articles.title: Is this how the NHS treats its own? 81-year-old man left outside Rochdale Infirmary for ten hours
articles.excerpt: An 81-year-old man spent around ten hours lying outside Rochdale Infirmary while members of the public repeatedly sought help. Rochdale Daily investigates what happened and asks who held responsibility for his care.
articles.content_html:
An 81-year-old man lay confused, incoherent and unable to stand outside the grounds of Rochdale Infirmary for around ten hours while members of the public desperately tried to persuade the emergency services, hospital staff and social care agencies to help him.

The disturbing incident was witnessed and filmed by the editor of Rochdale Daily, who saw passers-by provide the man with water, blankets, cushions, food and cardboard while repeated attempts were made to establish which public service had responsibility for his welfare.

The man was found lying on the ground near the hospital car park. He appeared unable to stand unaided and could rarely string together more than two words. He later told those attempting to assist him that he was 81 years old.

Security staff were monitoring the situation and informed members of the public they had contacted Greater Manchester Police. Officers did not arrive until approximately ten hours after the ordeal began.

Members of the public repeatedly attempted to request an ambulance. During those calls, callers say they were informed the man was barred from the ambulance service because of previous behaviour and because of other matters that could not be discussed due to data protection legislation.

The precise legal status of any restriction involving the man has not yet been independently confirmed. However, Rochdale Daily holds video footage of the day's events, including numerous conversations between witnesses, members of the public and staff.

Whatever may have happened previously, the man lying on the ground that day appeared incapable of posing any immediate threat. He was confused, unable to stand, largely unable to communicate and repeatedly soiled himself while lying outside the hospital.

Members of the public also attempted to contact Rochdale Council Adult Social Care, people believed to be relatives, homelessness organisations and local charities. Appeals were placed on Facebook asking whether anyone knew the gentleman or could help locate family members.

Some comments on social media suggested the man had brought the situation upon himself if he had previously abused NHS staff. One commenter wrote: "You don't get barred from the NHS for nothing."

No one should minimise the abuse suffered by NHS workers. Nurses, doctors, paramedics, receptionists and security staff face unacceptable levels of violence, intimidation and verbal abuse every day. Staff deserve protection, and where individuals genuinely pose a danger, organisations are entitled to implement appropriate safeguards.

But that was not the man witnessed by Rochdale Daily.

For hour after hour he remained lying on the ground, unable to stand, struggling to communicate and apparently incapable of caring for himself. Members of the public did not witness any aggression towards staff, security or those trying to help him.

Throughout the day, ambulance vehicles entered and left the hospital site. Witnesses attempted to flag them down, but the vehicles continued past. Others reportedly stopped only to explain they were unable to assist.

Approximately six hours into the incident, two nurses accompanied by hospital security entered the car park and spoke with those attempting to help the man.

According to the editor's contemporaneous video recording, the nurses stated they could not treat the gentleman unless the situation became a matter of "life or death".

When asked what 'life or death' would look like to an untrained member of the public, they replied: "We couldn't tell you."

Members of the public then asked whose duty of care the gentleman fell under if he died while no organisation would intervene. One member of staff replied: "Not you."

When pressed as to which organisation would carry responsibility if treatment continued to be refused, those present say no clear answer was given.

One nurse then stated that the gentleman's breathing would have to stop before intervention could take place.

The editor replied that she could not see him breathing. The nurse looked over the wall towards the gentleman and responded that his chest was rising and therefore he was breathing.

During the exchange, one nurse was recorded saying: "This is what you get when you're on it day and night."

When asked what she meant by the remark, no explanation was given.

Later in the incident, a person identifying themselves as a family member stated the gentleman had dementia. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that relationship or medical diagnosis.

A representative from Get Together After Serving CIC attended the scene after becoming aware of the incident and also attempted to secure medical assistance.

The representative said they were informed the gentleman was subject to a restraining order involving the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust and that members of the public would need to transport him outside the area before treatment could be sought elsewhere.

Rochdale Daily has requested clarification from the Trust regarding that alleged restriction.

Throughout the ordeal, members of the public continued caring for the gentleman. Bottles of water, blankets, cushions, cardboard and food were brought to make him more comfortable while people searched desperately for someone willing to take responsibility.

Among the organisations contacted, only Get Together After Serving CIC and Hebron Pentecostal Church attended to assist.

Approximately ten hours after the incident began, police officers attended the scene.

The following morning, disposable cups, bowls and cardboard still marked the place where the elderly man had spent much of the previous day.

This investigation is not an argument that NHS staff should tolerate abuse. They should not. Nor is it an argument that previous violent or abusive behaviour should simply be ignored.

It is, however, a question of safeguarding.

If an elderly man is confused, apparently incapable of caring for himself, unable to stand, repeatedly soiling himself and lying outside the grounds of a hospital, who has responsibility for protecting him?

If previous behaviour has resulted in restrictions, what emergency pathway exists when that same individual later appears to lack capacity or requires urgent medical assessment?

Those are questions Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, North West Ambulance Service, Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council's Adult Social Care service should now answer.

Rochdale Daily has contacted all relevant organisations for comment and will publish their responses in full when received.

Until then, one unavoidable question remains.

Is this how the NHS treats its own?

articles.title: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh appointed education minister: what his new role means for the borough
articles.excerpt: Paul Waugh remains Rochdale's MP while taking on a second role as a junior education minister. We examine his responsibilities, additional salary and what the appointment could mean locally.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has joined the Government as a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State in the Department for Education while continuing to represent the constituency in the House of Commons.

The appointment was formally confirmed as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's ministerial changes, with Mr Waugh taking up the post on 22 July 2026. Lucy Powell is the Secretary of State for Education and heads the department in which he will serve.

Mr Waugh now holds two connected public roles. He remains Rochdale's elected Member of Parliament, responsible for representing constituents, handling casework, holding surgeries, speaking on local issues and voting in the Commons. Alongside that work, he is now a junior government minister with responsibilities inside the Department for Education.

There is nothing unusual or constitutionally improper about an MP also serving as a minister. Most ministers in the House of Commons continue to represent their constituencies. His appointment does not create a vacancy, require a by-election or transfer his constituency responsibilities to another MP.

However, the ministerial job will substantially increase his workload. Ministers are expected to attend departmental meetings, study submissions from civil servants, help develop policy, answer parliamentary questions, take legislation through Parliament, meet education organisations and defend government decisions publicly.

That means constituents will reasonably expect reassurance that Rochdale casework and local representation will continue at the same level. Much of an MP's casework is managed by constituency and parliamentary staff, but Mr Waugh remains personally accountable to Rochdale voters and will still be expected to maintain a visible presence in the borough.

His precise policy portfolio has not yet been published by the Department for Education. The official government page currently confirms his rank and appointment but does not list a detailed set of responsibilities. It would therefore be premature to claim that he has direct control of a particular area such as schools, special educational needs, colleges or apprenticeships until the department formally allocates those duties.

As a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, he is one of the department's junior ministers. Such ministers commonly oversee a defined group of policies, represent the department during Commons debates, answer written and oral questions, meet professional bodies and work under the direction of the Education Secretary and more senior ministers.

The Department for Education is responsible for education and children's services in England. Its work includes early years provision, schools, teacher recruitment and retention, the curriculum, children's social care, further education, higher education, apprenticeships and skills.

The appointment could give Rochdale a stronger connection to national education decision-making, although a minister is required to make decisions for the country as a whole rather than favouring their own constituency.

Locally, there are several areas where residents and education providers will watch his work closely. These include special educational needs and disabilities, school funding, teacher recruitment, attendance, college provision, apprenticeships and support for children requiring speech, language and communication services.

Mr Waugh has previously highlighted Rochdale's work on SEND and early speech and language support. In June, after hosting a ministerial visit to the borough, he said his job was to ensure Rochdale received every penny and every bit of support it had earned. His new position places him inside the department responsible for much of that national policy, although ministerial rules may limit how directly he can intervene in individual local funding decisions.

His salary is also expected to increase if he claims the ministerial salary attached to the post. All MPs currently receive a basic annual salary of £98,599. The claimed additional salary for a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State serving in the Commons is £22,375.

That would produce total gross annual pay of £120,974 before tax, National Insurance and pension deductions. Ministerial salaries are separate from parliamentary expenses, which are intended to cover legitimate costs such as employing staff, running offices and travelling for parliamentary duties rather than providing additional personal income.

The increase is paid because ministerial office carries responsibilities beyond those of an ordinary backbench MP. Ministers are members of the Government and are bound by collective responsibility, meaning they are generally expected to support agreed government policy publicly or resign from office.

That obligation can occasionally create tension between the two roles. As Rochdale's MP, Mr Waugh is expected to raise local concerns and challenge decisions affecting his constituents. As a minister, he must also support the Government's education programme and comply with the Ministerial Code.

Having a minister as the local MP can provide greater access to senior figures and a deeper understanding of how government decisions are made. It does not, however, guarantee preferential funding or special treatment for the constituency. Decisions involving grants, schools and public bodies should continue to follow proper departmental processes.

Mr Waugh said he was "delighted" to be joining the Department for Education. His own website announced the appointment on 23 July, a day after the official government record says he took up the role.

The official announcement confirms that he joined an education team led by Lucy Powell, who became Education Secretary on 20 July. Other ministers in the department include Georgia Gould, Baroness Smith of Malvern and Josh MacAlister.

For Rochdale, the main test will be whether Mr Waugh can manage the demands of government while continuing to respond effectively to residents. Constituents should still contact his office about immigration cases, benefits, housing, public services and other matters requiring assistance from their MP.

His appointment raises Rochdale's profile within Westminster and places its MP closer to decisions affecting schools, children and skills across England. The title alone will not determine whether the borough benefits. That will depend on the responsibilities he is eventually given, the policies he helps deliver and whether residents continue to receive effective representation from their MP.

articles.title: Editorial: Justice remains unfinished in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: More than a decade after the Rochdale grooming gang scandal shocked Britain, the perpetrators have been jailed, reforms have been introduced and institutions have apologised. Yet for many survivors and residents, questions about accountability, trust and whether justice has truly been delivered remain unanswered.
articles.content_html:
More than a decade has passed since the Rochdale child sexual exploitation scandal exposed one of the gravest safeguarding failures in modern British history. The men responsible have been convicted and imprisoned, but the question that continues to confront Rochdale is whether justice ended with those convictions.

Successive independent inquiries have reached strikingly similar conclusions. Reviews by Parliament, local safeguarding bodies and independent investigators found that vulnerable children were repeatedly failed by institutions responsible for protecting them. Victims were too often viewed as making 'lifestyle choices' rather than recognised as children subjected to coercion, rape, trafficking and organised sexual exploitation. Information was not consistently shared between agencies, warning signs were missed, organised offending was underestimated and opportunities to intervene were repeatedly lost.

The testimony of survivors remains among the most compelling evidence of those failures. Girls described repeatedly reporting abuse only to be disbelieved, dismissed as troublesome teenagers or treated as willing participants in their own exploitation. Children who regularly went missing were returned to the same environments where offenders continued to target them. Independent reviews concluded that professionals frequently focused on victims' behaviour rather than the methods of coercion used by organised offenders.

The criminal justice system eventually delivered significant convictions. Operation Span resulted in nine men being convicted in 2012 for offences including rape, trafficking and conspiracy to engage in sexual activity with children. Further investigations have led to additional prosecutions linked to historic child sexual exploitation across Greater Manchester. Judges described the offending as calculated, organised and profoundly damaging, recognising that many victims would carry lifelong psychological trauma.

Yet convictions answered only one question: the guilt of the offenders. They did not answer why children were repeatedly failed before those prosecutions ever reached a courtroom.

The official inquiries found that the primary problem was not an absence of legislation. The criminal offences already existed. Rather, agencies failed to recognise organised grooming, safeguarding procedures were inconsistently applied, intelligence was not always effectively shared and vulnerable children were too often judged instead of protected. Some reviews also concluded that concerns about community tensions influenced professional decision-making in certain cases, although they stressed that institutional failures were complex and involved multiple contributing factors.

Political debate over those failures continues today. Sir Keir Starmer has consistently defended his record as Director of Public Prosecutions, pointing to reforms introduced after the Rochdale prosecutions that encouraged prosecutors to focus more closely on suspect behaviour rather than relying heavily on assessments of victim credibility. Nigel Farage has repeatedly argued that institutional accountability remains incomplete and has called for wider national inquiries into organised child sexual exploitation.

Independent MP Rupert Lowe commissioned his own inquiry into grooming gangs, arguing that previous investigations had failed to provide full transparency or accountability. Lowe's report calls for mandatory recording of offender ethnicity, stronger criminal justice responses, improved national data collection and further investigation into institutional failings. While his inquiry does not carry statutory authority, it has become part of the continuing national debate surrounding organised child sexual exploitation and institutional responsibility.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan also faced criticism after asking for clarification during a London Assembly meeting about what was meant by the phrase 'grooming gangs' before responding more broadly on child sexual exploitation. The exchange became part of the wider political discussion over how public authorities describe organised abuse and communicate with victims and the public.

There have unquestionably been improvements since the original scandal. Greater Manchester Police has established dedicated child sexual exploitation capabilities, multi-agency safeguarding arrangements have been strengthened, inspection reports have recognised improvements in identifying vulnerable children and historic offenders continue to face prosecution years after their crimes. Those reforms are significant and should not be dismissed.

However, reform is not the same as accountability.

For many survivors, organisational apologies and revised procedures have never fully addressed the institutional failures identified by successive inquiries. Former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver has repeatedly argued that child sexual exploitation remains a continuing threat and has warned against believing the lessons of Rochdale have been fully learned. She has consistently maintained that safeguarding depends not only on procedures but on professionals who are prepared to challenge assumptions, recognise organised exploitation and place children's welfare above institutional reputation.

Child sexual exploitation has not disappeared. Police forces across England and Wales continue to investigate organised grooming offences while offenders increasingly exploit social media, encrypted messaging platforms, online coercion and county lines criminality. Organised abuse evolves. Safeguarding must evolve with it.

The greatest lesson from Rochdale is not that Britain lacked the legal powers to prosecute offenders. It is that institutions repeatedly failed to use those powers when vulnerable children first asked for help. Children who should have been believed were doubted. Warning signs that should have triggered intervention were overlooked. Opportunities to prevent further abuse were lost.

Rochdale Borough Council has acknowledged profound institutional failings and apologised to survivors. Public bodies have accepted that serious mistakes were made, while successive reforms have sought to strengthen safeguarding and improve inter-agency cooperation. Those changes deserve recognition.

Whether they have fully restored public trust is another question entirely.

Justice cannot be measured solely by the length of prison sentences imposed on offenders. It is also measured by whether institutions learn from catastrophic failure, whether public officials accept responsibility when safeguarding collapses and whether every vulnerable child reporting abuse today can expect to be believed, protected and acted upon without hesitation.

Until survivors believe those standards have been achieved, and until the public is confident that institutional accountability carries meaningful consequences as well as organisational reform, many will continue to conclude that justice in Rochdale remains unfinished.

articles.title: Heat exposes challenges facing Rochdale workers and Britain’s ageing infrastructure
articles.excerpt: Temperatures are forecast to reach around 27°C in Rochdale today, while hotter conditions affect other parts of England. The weather is renewing questions about worker protection, climate change and whether Britain’s buildings and infrastructure are prepared for warmer summers.
articles.content_html:
Warm conditions are presenting renewed challenges for workers in Rochdale and across the country today, raising questions about whether climate change, inadequate infrastructure investment or a combination of both has left Britain poorly prepared for increasingly hot summers.

Temperatures in Rochdale are forecast to rise to approximately 27°C during the afternoon, with the hottest conditions expected between 3pm and 5pm. Although that is below the extreme temperatures recorded during previous heatwaves, it can still create difficult conditions inside poorly ventilated offices, factories, warehouses, workshops and vehicles.

Conditions are hotter in parts of southern and south-eastern England, where temperatures are significantly above those being experienced across Greater Manchester. The contrast means Britain is not facing identical conditions everywhere, but the national trend towards warmer and more frequent hot periods is placing increasing pressure on workplaces and public infrastructure.

Office workers can struggle in buildings with large windows, limited ventilation, sealed windows or insufficient cooling. Computers, lighting and large numbers of people can raise indoor temperatures beyond those recorded outside, leaving employees dealing with fatigue, headaches, dehydration and reduced concentration.

The risks are greater for people undertaking strenuous or outdoor work. Construction workers, roofers, landscapers, refuse collectors, delivery drivers, road crews, agricultural workers and utility engineers may be required to perform physically demanding tasks in direct sunlight while wearing heavy clothing or protective equipment.

Heat stress can develop when the body is unable to regulate its temperature effectively. Symptoms can include tiredness, dizziness, confusion, headaches, excessive sweating, muscle cramps and nausea. More serious cases can lead to heat exhaustion or heatstroke, requiring urgent medical attention.

There is no fixed maximum legal workplace temperature in Britain. The Health and Safety Executive says this is because workplaces vary considerably, with some industries naturally operating in hotter environments. Employers must nevertheless comply with health and safety law, maintain a reasonable working temperature, provide clean and fresh air and assess risks to employees.

For outdoor and physically demanding roles, sensible precautions can include access to drinking water, additional breaks, shaded rest areas, lighter clothing where safety permits and rescheduling the hardest work away from the hottest part of the day. Employers may also need to monitor staff for signs of heat stress and allow workers time to become accustomed to unusually warm conditions.

Whether Britain’s difficulties can be blamed on government underinvestment or climate change is not an either-or question.

Human-driven climate change is increasing the likelihood and severity of hot weather in Britain. Official figures published by the Office for National Statistics show that the average number of hot days during the decade from 2015 to 2024 was nearly double that recorded between 2005 and 2014. The most recent decade was also warmer than previous reference periods.

However, climate change does not explain why so many British workplaces, schools, hospitals, homes and transport systems struggle when temperatures rise. Much of the country’s built environment was designed for a historically cooler climate, while investment in ventilation, shading, insulation, urban trees and other forms of heat adaptation has not consistently kept pace with the changing risk.

The Climate Change Committee has repeatedly warned that Britain is inadequately prepared for the effects of a warmer climate. Its 2026 assessment said hotter heatwaves could eventually cause the overwhelming majority of existing homes to overheat without sufficient adaptation. Although that warning focused primarily on housing, many of the same construction and ventilation problems affect workplaces.

Successive governments of different political parties have therefore inherited and contributed to the problem. Britain’s exposure has developed over decades through ageing buildings, inconsistent adaptation policies and a planning system that has not always treated overheating as a central design concern.

The economic consequences are also significant. Experimental analysis by the Office for National Statistics estimated that hot days caused an average annual productivity loss of approximately £1.2 billion between 1998 and 2021, even after accounting for adaptation. Workers generally complete tasks more slowly in excessive heat, while employers may face disruption, additional breaks, equipment problems and higher cooling costs.

Urban areas can be particularly vulnerable because roads, roofs, concrete and other hard surfaces absorb heat during the day and release it slowly. Trees, parks, rivers and other green or blue spaces provide natural cooling, but their availability varies considerably between communities.

The challenge facing the Government is therefore twofold. Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions remains necessary to limit the severity of future warming, but adaptation is also required because some further climate change is already unavoidable.

That means improving building standards, retrofitting unsuitable properties, expanding tree cover, protecting green space and ensuring schools, hospitals, care facilities, transport networks and workplaces can remain safe during hot weather. Employers must also recognise that heat planning can no longer be treated as an exceptional response reserved for record-breaking temperatures.

Today’s weather in Rochdale is warm rather than unprecedented. Nevertheless, it provides another indication of a challenge that will become increasingly familiar. Climate change is making hot periods more likely, while inadequate preparation determines how disruptive and dangerous those periods become.

The evidence suggests both factors are responsible. The climate is changing, but Britain’s failure to adapt its workplaces and infrastructure quickly enough is increasing the burden placed on office staff, labourers and those whose jobs cannot simply be moved into an air-conditioned room.

articles.title: Is ketamine becoming a problem in Rochdale? Health leaders warn of a growing concern
articles.excerpt: Health professionals are warning of the growing harms associated with ketamine as national use rises. But what does the picture look like in Rochdale, and why are experts becoming increasingly concerned?
articles.content_html:
Ketamine was once regarded primarily as a nightclub drug, but health professionals, police and addiction specialists say its use has changed dramatically over the past decade. Increasingly, the drug is being used by younger people in a wider range of settings, prompting growing concern about its impact on physical and mental health.

While there is no publicly available evidence to suggest Rochdale has a ketamine problem significantly worse than other parts of Greater Manchester, local authorities recognise substance misuse as an important public health issue and have included drug-related harm as a key priority in the borough's long-term prevention strategy. Rochdale's Preventing Drug and Alcohol Harm Strategy highlights the need to reduce drug-related harm through prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery services.

Ketamine is a Class B controlled drug in the UK. Originally developed as a medical anaesthetic, it produces feelings of detachment and hallucinations when used recreationally. In recent years, it has become increasingly popular because it is often cheaper than cocaine and MDMA, while users mistakenly believe it to be a 'safer' drug.

National evidence suggests that perception is dangerously wrong. The Home Office's latest wastewater analysis estimates ketamine consumption has increased substantially in England in recent years, making it one of the country's most commonly consumed illegal drugs after cocaine.

Doctors are particularly concerned about the long-term physical effects. Repeated ketamine use can cause irreversible damage to the bladder and urinary tract, a condition sometimes referred to as 'ketamine bladder' or ketamine-induced cystitis. Heavy users may experience severe pain, frequent urination, bleeding and, in the most serious cases, permanent bladder damage requiring reconstructive surgery. Medical specialists have reported a significant increase in young patients requiring treatment for these complications.

Mental health professionals also warn that regular ketamine use can lead to dependency, memory problems, anxiety, depression and episodes of psychosis in some individuals. Because the drug affects perception and coordination, users are also at increased risk of accidents, injuries and dangerous behaviour while intoxicated.

Locally, Rochdale Borough Council's Joint Strategic Needs Assessment identifies substance misuse among young adults as an ongoing public health challenge. Hospital admission rates linked to substance misuse among young people remain broadly similar to the national average, while the council notes that vulnerable groups are at greater risk of developing drug-related problems.

Although official figures are not routinely broken down by individual drug at borough level, professionals working in addiction services across Greater Manchester say ketamine now features far more frequently than it did a decade ago. Nationally, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs concluded earlier this year that misuse is increasing and recommended strengthening education, prevention and treatment services while keeping ketamine as a Class B drug.

Parents are encouraged to be aware of the warning signs. These can include sudden mood changes, poor concentration, unexplained urinary problems, nosebleeds caused by snorting powder, secrecy around friendships, declining school or college attendance and unexplained financial difficulties. None of these signs alone necessarily indicate drug use, but experts advise early conversations and support where concerns exist.

Support is available for anyone struggling with drug use. Rochdale residents can access confidential help through local drug and alcohol treatment services without fear of judgement. Health professionals stress that seeking support early greatly improves the chances of recovery and helps prevent long-term physical damage.

The message from health leaders is clear. While ketamine may still carry an image as a recreational party drug, the evidence increasingly shows it can have devastating consequences for both physical and mental health. Prevention, education and early intervention remain the most effective ways of protecting young people across Rochdale borough from the lasting harm associated with its misuse.

articles.title: GCSE results day 2026: What Rochdale parents need to know – and why one set of grades doesn't define a future
articles.excerpt: From college offers to apprenticeships and changing employer expectations, here's everything Rochdale parents need to know before GCSE results day.
articles.content_html:
Thousands of teenagers across Rochdale borough will soon collect one of the most important envelopes of their young lives as GCSE results day approaches.

For many families, results day brings a mixture of excitement, nerves and uncertainty. Parents naturally want the best for their children, but education experts say GCSEs are increasingly becoming just one of several routes into higher education, apprenticeships and long-term careers rather than the single deciding factor they were once perceived to be.

This year's GCSE results will be released on Thursday 20 August, with schools across Rochdale opening to allow students to collect their grades and speak with teachers about their next steps. Students will receive provisional results before certificates are issued later in the year.

For many teenagers, the next destination has already been decided through conditional offers from sixth forms and colleges. Most colleges will honour offers provided students meet the required grades, while admissions teams are usually available on results day to discuss alternatives if results are different from those expected.

Compared with a decade ago, today's post-16 education landscape is far more flexible. Alongside traditional A Levels, students can now choose from T Levels, vocational qualifications, apprenticeships and technical training, giving young people far more options depending on their interests and career ambitions. Greater Manchester has also continued expanding the Greater Manchester Baccalaureate (MBacc), designed to place technical education on an equal footing with academic study while creating clearer pathways into local industries.

Parents often ask whether GCSEs still matter.

The answer is yes—but perhaps not in the way they once did.

GCSEs remain important because they open doors. Most sixth forms, colleges, universities and apprenticeship providers require passes in English Language and Mathematics, while many A Level courses ask for a minimum grade in the subject students wish to study. Employers also continue to value GCSEs as evidence of literacy, numeracy and commitment, particularly when recruiting school leavers with little previous work experience. Ofqual has described GCSEs as a 'passport to opportunity', providing access to further education, apprenticeships and employment.

However, the employment market has changed dramatically. Increasingly, recruiters say experience, practical skills, communication, teamwork and attitude become far more important than GCSE grades as careers progress.

Recruitment specialists consistently report that while GCSEs may be used as an initial screening tool for younger applicants, employers recruiting experienced candidates are far more interested in work history, achievements, technical skills and professional qualifications. In sectors such as construction, logistics, digital technology, engineering, health and social care, apprenticeships have become an increasingly respected route into well-paid careers.

That does not mean students should dismiss their exams. Strong GCSE results can provide greater choice and flexibility, particularly for competitive sixth forms, universities and professional careers such as medicine, dentistry and law. But equally, disappointing grades do not prevent someone building a successful future.

Parents are also encouraged to remember that results day is only one moment in a much longer journey. Colleges regularly help students who narrowly miss entry requirements by suggesting alternative courses, foundation programmes or vocational pathways that still lead towards the same career goals.

For students who do not achieve the grade 4 pass in English or Mathematics, the law requires them to continue studying those subjects alongside most post-16 courses until they achieve the qualification or turn 18. While this can initially feel disappointing, many students successfully improve their grades during college.

Perhaps the biggest change in recent years has been the growing recognition that success comes in many different forms. University is no longer viewed as the only prestigious route after school. articles.title: Lives cut short: Remembering the young people lost on Rochdale's roads
articles.excerpt: A look at the tragic loss of young lives on Rochdale's roads since 2020 and the ongoing efforts to improve road safety across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Every fatal road traffic collision leaves behind grieving families, devastated friends and communities asking whether more could have been done to prevent another life being cut short.

Since 2020, a number of young people have tragically lost their lives on roads across Rochdale borough. While every collision has had its own unique circumstances, each has served as a stark reminder that road safety is not simply about statistics – it is about sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, classmates and friends whose futures were taken away far too soon.

One of the most heartbreaking incidents came in April 2025 when six-year-old Myra Tahseen died after being struck by a vehicle on Ashfield Road. Emergency services fought to save her, but she sadly died from her injuries. The tragedy prompted an outpouring of grief across Rochdale, with floral tributes left at the scene and specialist officers supporting her family while investigations continued.

Although fatalities involving children and young people are thankfully rare, they remain one of the leading causes of death for those aged between five and nineteen across the United Kingdom. Rochdale's own Joint Strategic Needs Assessment highlights that land transport collisions remain among the principal causes of death for young people and reports that the borough's rate of children killed or seriously injured on the roads is around 15 per 100,000 population.

Behind every fatal collision lies a complex combination of circumstances. Excessive speed, distraction, impairment through drink or drugs, failure to wear seatbelts, poor weather, inexperience and momentary lapses in concentration can all contribute to devastating outcomes. Road safety experts consistently stress that many serious collisions are preventable through safer driving behaviour.

Young drivers remain disproportionately represented in serious road collisions nationwide. Inexperience, overconfidence and risk-taking behaviour can all increase the likelihood of being involved in a collision, particularly during the first years after passing a driving test. Equally, young pedestrians and cyclists are among the most vulnerable road users, particularly near schools, residential estates and busy roads.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit continues to investigate every fatal collision thoroughly, examining witness statements, CCTV, vehicle data, road conditions and forensic evidence to establish exactly what happened. These investigations often continue for many months before an inquest is held, allowing families to receive answers and, where appropriate, criminal proceedings to take place.

Road safety is not solely the responsibility of drivers. Pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and passengers all have a role to play in reducing risk. Simple decisions such as slowing down in residential areas, putting mobile phones away, wearing seatbelts correctly, using pedestrian crossings where available and remaining alert around schools can make a significant difference.

Across Rochdale borough, organisations continue to work together to improve road safety through engineering improvements, education campaigns, enforcement against dangerous driving and community awareness initiatives. Every serious collision provides lessons that can help prevent future tragedies.

For the families who have lost loved ones, however, those lessons come at an unimaginable cost. Birthdays go uncelebrated, empty seats remain at family tables and communities continue to remember young lives that ended far too soon.

The hope shared by police, road safety campaigners and residents alike is that by learning from these tragedies, encouraging responsible driving and remaining vigilant on every journey, fewer families will have to experience the heartbreak of losing someone they love on Rochdale's roads.

articles.title: Residents raise concerns over anti-social behaviour around Kingsway
articles.excerpt: Residents and businesses are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour around Kingsway, with police identifying retail crime, ASB and road safety as neighbourhood priorities.

Residents and businesses around the Kingsway area of Rochdale are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour, saying a minority of offenders are affecting what is otherwise one of the borough's busiest retail and employment destinations.

Kingsway has undergone significant regeneration over the past two decades, transforming into a major business and retail hub with national retailers, industrial estates, distribution centres and hundreds of jobs. Thousands of people visit the area every day to shop, work and access nearby facilities.

However, some residents and businesses say issues including nuisance behaviour, shoplifting, groups congregating outside retail premises, dangerous driving and road safety concerns have become increasingly noticeable in recent years.

Greater Manchester Police has identified retail crime at Kingsway Retail Park, anti-social behaviour and road safety as neighbourhood policing priorities for the area. Officers say they have carried out targeted operations against shoplifting, increased patrols and undertaken road traffic enforcement to tackle motorists committing offences.

Police have confirmed that numerous arrests have been made for shoplifting at Morrisons in recent months, while dedicated traffic operations have also been carried out along Kingsway to improve road safety. Regular police surgeries are also being held at Kingsway Retail Park to allow residents and businesses to discuss local concerns directly with neighbourhood officers.

For businesses operating on Kingsway, anti-social behaviour can have a wider economic impact. Retailers say persistent shoplifting, disorder and nuisance behaviour place additional pressure on staff while affecting customer confidence. Many businesses have invested heavily in CCTV, security staff and crime prevention measures, working alongside Greater Manchester Police to identify prolific offenders.

Residents have also highlighted concerns over speeding, dangerous driving and the use of modified vehicles on Kingsway, particularly during evenings. Although the vast majority of motorists use the road responsibly, police say road safety remains one of their key neighbourhood priorities alongside tackling retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Community safety experts say anti-social behaviour often requires more than enforcement alone. Alongside visible policing, long-term solutions typically involve youth engagement, support for vulnerable individuals, environmental improvements, partnership working with businesses and swift action against repeat offenders.

There have been encouraging signs elsewhere in Rochdale. Greater Manchester Police recently reported significant reductions in anti-social behaviour and wider crime within Rochdale town centre following the introduction of Operation Tetbury, a partnership initiative combining targeted policing with regeneration and community engagement. Officers say anti-social behaviour in the town centre fell by more than 30 per cent during the first year of the operation.

Many residents hope a similarly proactive approach around Kingsway will continue to improve the area, ensuring it remains an attractive destination for shoppers, businesses and investors.

The overwhelming majority of people visiting Kingsway do so without experiencing any problems, and local businesses continue to invest confidently in the area. Nevertheless, residents say continued police visibility, partnership working and prompt action against those responsible for anti-social behaviour will be essential to protecting one of Rochdale's most important commercial centres.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing anti-social behaviour or criminal activity to report it online, by calling 101, or by dialling 999 if there is an immediate risk to life or a crime is in progress.

articles.title: One man became one walk – now Rochdale's Men Walking and Talking group hopes others will join him
articles.excerpt: A new Men Walking and Talking group has launched in Rochdale, offering men a safe, informal place to meet, walk and talk as organisers hope to tackle loneliness, improve mental wellbeing and reduce the stigma surrounding men's mental health.
articles.content_html:
A simple walk can sometimes be the first step towards changing a life.

That's the message behind Men Walking and Talking, the national Community Interest Company helping men support one another through conversation, companionship and fresh air. The organisation recently launched its Rochdale group, offering a free weekly walk where men can meet without pressure, judgement or the expectation that they have to talk if they don't want to. The walks take place every Thursday evening from Rochdale Cenotaph and are open to all men, with no booking required.

The Rochdale group's organiser recently reflected on one of the challenges facing any new community initiative – sometimes the first person to turn up is the organiser themselves. In recent weeks he has often found himself walking alone, but says he'll continue turning up each Thursday because he believes someone who needs the group will eventually come.

That quiet determination reflects the purpose of Men Walking and Talking. The organisation was founded on the belief that men often find it easier to open up while walking side by side than sitting face-to-face. There is no expectation to share personal struggles, but there is always the opportunity to chat if someone feels ready.

Research has consistently shown that regular physical activity can play an important role in supporting mental wellbeing. Walking outdoors has been linked to reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression, lower stress levels and improved mood. Spending time in nature, exercising regularly and building social connections can all contribute positively to mental health, while loneliness and social isolation are recognised risk factors for poor mental wellbeing.

For many men, however, talking about mental health remains difficult. Although attitudes have improved in recent years, stigma still prevents some people from seeking support. Organisations such as Men Walking and Talking aim to break down those barriers by creating informal spaces where conversation develops naturally rather than feeling like therapy.

The need for initiatives like this remains significant. Suicide continues to be one of the leading causes of death among men under the age of 50 in the UK, with men accounting for around three-quarters of all registered suicides nationally. Behind every statistic are families, friends and communities left dealing with unimaginable loss.

Groups such as Men Walking and Talking cannot replace professional mental health services, but they can provide something equally valuable – connection. A friendly face, a shared walk and the knowledge that someone else understands can make a real difference for people who may otherwise feel isolated.

Community is another important part of the group's mission. Beyond improving physical fitness, regular walks help people build friendships, strengthen local networks and create a sense of belonging. Many participants across the country say they first attended for the walk but kept returning because of the people they met along the way.

The Rochdale organiser hopes more local men will consider giving the group a try. There is no membership, no pressure to speak and no expectation to explain why you've come. Whether someone wants to chat openly, listen quietly or simply enjoy an evening walk with others, they are welcome.

If you are struggling with your mental health, you do not have to face it alone. If you are having thoughts of suicide or feel unable to keep yourself safe, call 999 immediately or go to your nearest Accident and Emergency department. You can also contact Samaritans free of charge on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, or reach out to CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably) on 0800 58 58 58 or through its webchat service. If your situation is not an emergency but you need support, speak to your GP or contact NHS 111 for advice.

Sometimes the hardest part is taking the first step. For one Rochdale volunteer, that first step has meant walking alone while waiting for others to join him. He hopes that, before long, those solitary walks will become conversations shared with men who simply needed someone to walk beside.

Reports at the time indicated he was subsequently banned from the gym.

Online content

These include the Tartaria conspiracy theory, claims that the Apollo Moon landings were faked, the so-called Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory, and claims that mountains are the fossilised remains of enormous petrified creatures.

The Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory has been widely rejected by historians and researchers and is commonly associated with antisemitic conspiracy narratives.

Many of Margerison's videos challenge established historical, archaeological and scientific consensus and have generated substantial debate and criticism online.

Police investigation

Scottish police have confirmed officers received complaints and are reviewing the available material to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

articles.title: Reform's strongest showing yet reshapes Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Labour retained the Greater Manchester mayoralty, but Reform UK's strongest regional performance to date has reshaped the political landscape and established the party as the city's principal opposition force.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester has elected a new mayor, with Labour's Bev Craig succeeding Andy Burnham after winning the mayoral by-election. While Labour retained the office, one of the election's defining stories was the emergence of Reform UK as the city's principal opposition force, with Sian Astley delivering the party's strongest performance in a Greater Manchester-wide contest to date.

Craig secured 309,525 votes in the final round, representing 66.3 per cent of the vote, while Reform UK's Sian Astley received 157,178 votes, or 33.7 per cent. The result followed a second-round count after no candidate achieved an outright majority of first-preference votes.

Astley's campaign marked a significant moment for Reform UK in Greater Manchester. Standing on a platform centred on neighbourhood policing, transparency in regional government, public spending and directing more investment towards towns across all ten boroughs, she introduced the party's message to hundreds of thousands of voters and established Reform as Labour's most significant electoral challenger in the city-region.

The first-preference vote illustrated that shift. Astley secured 111,928 votes, comfortably finishing ahead of every other opposition candidate. While Labour maintained its lead, Reform's result demonstrated that many voters are now looking beyond the traditional political parties, reflecting wider political changes seen across England over recent years.

The election also highlighted the scale of the challenge facing every political party in reconnecting with the electorate. Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the Greater Manchester mayoralty was introduced in 2017. More than three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot despite the mayor holding responsibility for transport, policing, housing, regeneration, adult education funding and significant economic investment across the region.

For many observers, that figure raises important questions about public engagement with devolved government. The office of Mayor of Greater Manchester has become one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster, yet millions of residents continue to feel disconnected from regional politics. Whether the low turnout reflected election fatigue, limited awareness of the mayor's powers or wider political dissatisfaction will no doubt be debated in the months ahead.

Astley's campaign also carried wider historical significance. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was created in 2017. Although that milestone was not reached, her candidacy demonstrated the increasing diversity of those seeking senior political office within the city-region.

The campaign itself was notable for the issues it placed at the centre of debate. Reform UK argued for greater scrutiny of Combined Authority spending, more visible neighbourhood policing, improved road maintenance and stronger accountability within regional government. Labour focused on continuing the Bee Network, delivering new housing and building on the devolution settlement developed under Andy Burnham. Voters were therefore presented with two distinctly different visions for Greater Manchester's future.

For Rochdale residents, the outcome will have practical consequences regardless of political preference. The mayor oversees Greater Manchester Police through the Police and Crime Commissioner powers, shapes strategic transport investment including the Bee Network, influences regeneration funding and represents the region in negotiations with central government. Decisions taken over the next four years will directly affect communities throughout Rochdale borough.

Although Labour retains control of the mayoralty, the election demonstrated that Greater Manchester's political landscape is becoming increasingly competitive. Reform UK's performance suggests future elections may no longer be defined by a straightforward Labour contest, with Astley's campaign establishing the party as a credible challenger across much of the city-region.

Attention now turns from campaigning to governing. Bev Craig inherits responsibility for one of England's largest devolved administrations at a time of financial pressure, growing demands on public services and continuing debate over transport, policing and housing. At the same time, Reform UK leaves the campaign with increased visibility, a larger regional profile and the opportunity to build on its strongest Greater Manchester result to date ahead of future elections.

articles.title: Labour Wins GM Election: a narrow mandate, a continuity platform, and a borough still waiting
articles.excerpt: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig takes office as Mayor of Greater Manchester having won 309,525 votes to Sian Astley's 157,178, a second-round margin of 66.3 per cent to 33.7. She inherits transport, policing, housing and skills powers assembled over nine years, and a budget running to billions.

Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the office was created. Craig's total amounts to roughly one in seven of those entitled to vote. That is not a criticism of her — she did not choose the date, and no candidate can compel people to the polls. But it could set the stage for what follows. A mayor with powers of this scale and a base of active consent this narrow should expect close questioning, and would be wise to welcome it.

The contest was also tighter on first preferences than the final figure implies. Neither candidate reached 50 per cent outright, which is why a second count was needed. Reform UK finished second across all ten boroughs at its first serious attempt at this office. Labour has held the mayoralty since it was created; it has now been taken to a second round in its strongest English region.

The substantive disagreement is about continuity. Craig campaigned on carrying forward the programme she inherits — the Bee Network, housing delivery, neighbourhood policing, further devolution talks with government. For Manchester that is a reasonable prospectus. For Rochdale it is the least attractive offer available, because the arrangement now being continued has not worked here. The borough sits at the end of a Metrolink line, with a rail service that has been unreliable for years, contributing to a city-region strategy whose most visible results are concentrated closer to the centre.

There is a fair answer to that, and it deserves stating. Craig's supporters argue that a Labour mayor working with a Labour government is better placed to win further devolved powers and the money attached to them, and that Rochdale gains more from that than from opposition. It is a serious argument. It is also a testable one, and the test is whether the borough's share of transport and housing investment rises over the next four years or stays where it is.

On policing, the mayor holds the powers of a Police and Crime Commissioner, which makes this the area where the office touches residents most directly. Our measure will be simple and public: response times, charge rates, and whether people who report a crime in this borough hear back. Those figures are published. We intend to use them.

The by-election itself carried a cost — the 2024 mayoral contest cost taxpayers £4.7 million, and this one is expected to run to millions again. That is a consequence of a sitting mayor leaving mid-term for Westminster, not of anything the new mayor did. But it is money spent on an election in which three quarters of the electorate did not participate, and it is reasonable to ask what the region got for it.

Craig begins with substantial powers and a quiet electorate. We will report what she does with them, and judge her on what changes in this borough rather than on what is announced in Manchester.

articles.title: Could Greater Manchester elect its first woman mayor?
articles.excerpt: As the Greater Manchester mayoral count continues, Sian Astley could become the first woman to hold the office if elected, marking a historic milestone for the city-region's devolved government.

As Greater Manchester awaits the declaration of its mayoral by-election, one potential milestone has emerged alongside the political contest. If Reform UK candidate Sian Astley is elected, she would become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was established in 2017.

The mayoralty has grown into one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster. The successful candidate will oversee transport through the Bee Network, hold the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, help shape housing and regeneration policy, manage elements of adult education funding and represent Greater Manchester in discussions with central government over future devolution.

Astley entered politics after a career in business and property development before winning election as a councillor in Manchester. Her mayoral campaign has focused on transparency in regional government, neighbourhood policing, public spending and directing investment across all ten Greater Manchester boroughs. She has argued that communities outside Manchester city centre should receive a greater share of future funding and infrastructure projects.

If elected, Astley would follow Tony Lloyd and Andy Burnham, both of whom held the office before her. While women have led councils and held senior public roles across Greater Manchester, the directly elected mayoralty has so far only been occupied by men.

The possibility of the city-region electing its first female mayor has attracted attention beyond party politics. Supporters describe it as an opportunity to broaden representation in one of England's most significant devolved offices, while political opponents have continued to debate her policies rather than the historical significance of her candidacy.

The election itself follows Andy Burnham's departure after almost a decade in office. During that time, the role expanded considerably through devolution agreements, making the mayor responsible for decisions that affect millions of residents across Rochdale, Manchester, Salford, Bolton, Bury, Oldham, Stockport, Tameside, Trafford and Wigan.

Whatever the outcome, the by-election represents a significant moment for Greater Manchester. Voters are choosing not only who will lead the combined authority but also who will inherit responsibility for some of the region's most important public services. If the result confirms Astley's election, it would also mark the first time a woman has held the office, adding a new chapter to the history of Greater Manchester's devolved government.

articles.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Rochdale Feel Good Festival 2026
articles.excerpt: From headliners and ticket prices to travel, parking, accessibility and the latest weather forecast, here's everything you need to know before Rochdale Feel Good Festival returns next weekend.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest annual music event returns next weekend, with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the town centre for the 2026 Feel Good Festival. Headlined by BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, alongside indie favourites Ash and Starsailor, the festival promises a full day of live music, street entertainment, food, drink and family activities, continuing a tradition that has become one of Greater Manchester's most successful free town centre festivals.

Now celebrating its 15th edition, the Feel Good Festival has grown from a small local music event into one of the highlights of the borough's cultural calendar. Previous festivals have welcomed acts including Ocean Colour Scene, Razorlight, Feeder, The Coral, Scouting For Girls, The Fratellis, Heather Small, Cast, Toploader, Badly Drawn Boy, The Feeling, The Lightning Seeds and The Beat, attracting visitors from across the North West and providing a welcome boost to Rochdale's hospitality and retail sectors.

This year's main stage takes place in the stunning surroundings of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall Square on Saturday, 8 August. Headlining the evening is Gabrielle, whose catalogue includes classics such as Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She is joined by Ash, Starsailor, funk and soul outfit The Allergies and Manchester indie rising star Alex Spencer, with additional performances throughout the day and live entertainment continuing across numerous indoor venues around the town centre. Most indoor performances remain completely free, with only the main stage requiring a ticket.

Festival organisers have continued their commitment to making the event affordable. Early bird tickets sold out quickly at £15 before subsequent release phases increased to £25, £30, £35 and the final allocation at £45 plus booking fees. VIP upgrades remain available for those wanting premium viewing areas and additional hospitality. Every ticket includes a reusable festival cup as part of the organisers' ongoing efforts to reduce single-use plastics.

Entertainment begins from 11.30am and continues until approximately 10.45pm, with the main stage located in Rochdale Town Hall Square. Festival organisers recommend arriving early to collect wristbands, avoid queues and enjoy the wide variety of free entertainment taking place throughout the town centre before the headline performances begin.

Getting to the festival is expected to be straightforward thanks to Rochdale's excellent public transport links. Organisers are encouraging visitors to use public transport where possible, with Metrolink trams running directly into Rochdale town centre and Northern train services providing regular connections from Manchester Victoria, Leeds, Halifax and Blackburn. Numerous Bee Network bus services also stop within a short walk of the festival site, while taxi ranks will operate throughout the day and into the evening to assist those travelling home after the headline acts.

Drivers are advised to allow extra time, as town centre car parks are expected to fill quickly. Public parking is available at several locations including The Esplanade, Riverside, Baillie Street and other nearby council-operated car parks, although temporary road closures around the Town Hall may affect access during the festival. Visitors are encouraged to check council travel advice before setting off.

Accessibility continues to be a major focus for organisers. A dedicated accessible viewing platform will be available within the main stage arena for wheelchair users and those with mobility issues, while British Sign Language interpreters will be present during main stage performances. Accessible toilets are provided both within the outdoor festival site and nearby indoor venues. Essential companion tickets are available free of charge for eligible visitors, assistance dogs are welcome and a quiet space will also be available for anyone requiring time away from the crowds.

Toilets will be located throughout the festival site, including accessible facilities, with additional public conveniences available inside participating venues. Festival stewards will be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors and provide directions around the event.

Food has become almost as popular as the music in recent years, with dozens of traders expected to serve everything from gourmet burgers and wood-fired pizzas to Asian street food, desserts and locally produced refreshments. Although organisers have not published official bar prices, visitors should expect festival-standard pricing broadly comparable with similar outdoor events across Greater Manchester. Outside alcohol is not permitted inside the main stage arena, although sealed soft drinks and water may be allowed subject to festival rules. Visitors are encouraged to support local independent food and drink traders operating throughout the event.

The weather currently looks favourable for festival-goers, with forecasts suggesting a mostly sunny day, light winds and temperatures reaching around 19°C. While conditions can always change, current forecasts indicate comfortable weather for spending the day outdoors, although organisers still recommend bringing sunscreen, drinking plenty of water and packing a light waterproof just in case the British summer has other ideas.

Beyond the music, the Feel Good Festival has become an important economic event for Rochdale. Thousands of visitors pass through the town centre every year, providing a significant boost to local restaurants, pubs, cafés, hotels and independent retailers. The festival also showcases Rochdale's cultural offer following the restoration of the Grade I-listed Town Hall and supports the borough's wider ambitions to attract more visitors and investment.

The festival is organised on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council with support from Rochdale Development Agency, ticket sales and sponsorship from local businesses and community partners. Over the years, numerous organisations have supported the event, helping to ensure it remains one of the North West's best-value music festivals while continuing to celebrate local talent alongside nationally recognised artists.

For anyone planning to attend, organisers recommend arriving early, using public transport where possible, checking travel updates before setting off and allowing extra time to move between venues. Whether you're there to see Gabrielle, discover new artists, enjoy the food village or simply soak up the atmosphere in Rochdale town centre, this year's Feel Good Festival looks set to continue one of the borough's proudest summer traditions.

articles.title: Who is Sian Astley? The businesswoman hoping to reshape Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Businesswoman, councillor and Reform UK's Greater Manchester mayoral candidate, Sian Astley has rapidly become one of the region's most talked-about political figures. Here's a closer look at her background, campaign and policies.
articles.content_html:
Until recently, Sian Astley was better known for property development and television appearances than frontline politics. Today, the Reform UK councillor is one of the party's most recognisable figures in Greater Manchester, having been selected to contest the mayoral by-election following Andy Burnham's departure from the role.

Astley's political rise has been rapid. Earlier this year she won the Baguley ward on Manchester City Council, ending more than half a century of Labour representation in the area. She now leads Reform UK's group on the council, giving the party a significantly higher profile in one of Labour's traditional strongholds.

Away from politics, Astley runs a design and property business and has appeared on national television discussing housing, renovation and landlord issues. A graduate of the University of Manchester, she has frequently argued that politics benefits from representatives with experience outside Westminster and local government. Speaking after her selection, she said she wanted 'real people with real life experience' making decisions that affect local communities.

Her campaign centred on a message that Greater Manchester has become too heavily dominated by a single political party. Astley argued that decades of Labour control across many parts of the city-region had reduced scrutiny and accountability, claiming residents deserved greater transparency over how public money is spent. Reform UK's campaign presented itself as offering robust opposition rather than continuity.

One of Astley's headline pledges was to review major contracts and spending decisions taken during Andy Burnham's time as mayor. She proposed examining combined authority spending on development projects, reviewing expenditure connected to the abandoned Clean Air Zone proposals and increasing public access to information about regional decision-making. Reform UK argued that taxpayers should have greater visibility over how devolved budgets are allocated.

Crime and community safety formed another central pillar of her campaign. Reform UK proposed increasing police visibility, taking a tougher approach to knife crime, expanding the use of stop-and-search powers, tackling shoplifting and antisocial behaviour, and prioritising neighbourhood policing. The party argued that public confidence in policing had declined and that stronger enforcement was needed to improve safety across Greater Manchester.

Transport policy also featured prominently. Astley criticised spending on what she described as underused cycling infrastructure and opposed introducing additional charges on motorists. She argued that investment should be distributed more evenly across Greater Manchester rather than concentrating predominantly on Manchester city centre, saying outer boroughs such as Rochdale, Bolton and Wigan deserved a larger share of future transport and regeneration funding.

Economic development was another recurring theme. Reform UK's manifesto called for greater support for high streets, road maintenance and local businesses, alongside efforts to reduce what the party described as unnecessary expenditure within the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Astley argued that improving everyday infrastructure would deliver more visible benefits to residents than prestige projects concentrated in the regional centre.

Immigration also featured in Reform UK's regional campaign, although many aspects remain matters for national government rather than the Mayor of Greater Manchester. The party proposed greater transparency around asylum accommodation, opposition to the use of hotels for asylum seekers and stronger cooperation with councils on community impacts. Supporters argued these proposals reflected public concerns, while critics questioned how much influence a metro mayor could realistically exercise over national immigration policy.

Like every candidate in the contest, Astley also faced criticism during the campaign. Political opponents challenged the practicality of some of Reform UK's proposals, particularly where powers rest with Westminster rather than the combined authority. There was also discussion after Astley withdrew from one mayoral hustings organised by The Mill, with Astley stating she objected to the exclusion of independent candidate Marcus Farmer, while organisers maintained their own position on participation.

Whatever the election result, few would dispute that Astley has helped establish Reform UK as a more visible force in Greater Manchester politics. Her victory in Baguley demonstrated the party's ability to make gains in areas long considered Labour strongholds, and her mayoral campaign brought Reform's message before voters across all ten boroughs.

The longer-term question is whether that momentum can be sustained. Metro mayoral elections often provide smaller parties with greater exposure than they receive during local elections, but converting visibility into long-term electoral success is a more difficult task. Reform UK will likely judge Astley's campaign not solely by the final vote share but by whether it has expanded the party's organisation, profile and support across Greater Manchester.

As Greater Manchester enters a post-Burnham political era, Astley's campaign reflects wider changes taking place in British politics.
